transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

Probably not. A loud buzz or hum from an induction hob on a high setting is one of the most common things people worry about, and it's usually normal. Induction works by pushing a strong, fast-changing magnetic field into the pan. At high power that makes the pan's metal, and especially the layers in a multi-layer (clad) base, vibrate slightly. A big stockpot full of water on high is the classic case, because it's a large pan drawing a lot of power. The noise usually comes from the pan, not the hob, and it often gets quieter as you turn the power down. You may also hear a cooling fan running during and after cooking, and clicking at low settings. Both are normal. The likely causes, most likely first:
1. Normal induction noise from the pan at high power.
2. The pan itself making it worse, for example a slightly warped or domed base, a base layer that's coming loose, or a pan that's much bigger or smaller than the zone.
3. Much less likely, a developing fault in that zone's coil or power electronics, or the cooling fan. A few quick checks will tell these apart:
1. Turn the power down a few steps while it's buzzing. If the noise drops off, that's normal induction behaviour.
2. Try a different flat-bottomed pan on the same zone on high. If it's much quieter, the stockpot is the source. You can also try the stockpot on another zone. If it buzzes on every zone, it's the pan.
3. Once the pot is cool and empty, check its base. Put it upside down on the worktop and lay a straight edge across the base. A rock or a gap, or a rattle from the base layer, means the pan will hum more. Using the pan with water in it, and centred on a zone that suits its size, often helps.
4. If the hob has a boost or power-boost setting, try one level below it. Boost is often the noisiest setting. It would count as a fault rather than normal noise if you notice any of these:
• Loud cracking or snapping
• A burning or hot-plastic smell
• Sparks
• The hob cutting out or showing an error code
• A grinding or rattling noise from underneath that continues with no pan on
• The noise happening with every pan, even at low settings If any of those appear, stop using that zone and switch the hob off at its isolator. That would need an engineer, as the power electronics inside an induction hob aren't owner-serviceable.

I tried a few of those. It's much quieter at 6 and below, and it happens on every zone with that pot. My heavy cast iron pot is quiet, but a cheap frying pan I have is noisy too. There are no error codes and no cutting out, no burning smell and no rattling. I do get a slight crackle sometimes. The fan whirs for a minute or two after I switch off. The pot has a sandwich base that's maybe slightly smaller than the zone ring, but I haven't checked whether it's flat. Does that sound like normal noise from the pan?

Yes, that sounds like normal pan noise, and I'm fairly confident about it. 1. It's much quieter at 6 and below. Induction hum rises and falls with power.
2. It happens on every zone, but only with certain pans. A fault would usually be tied to one zone, not one pan.
3. The heavy cast iron pot is quiet. Solid one-piece iron vibrates very little. Sandwich bases and thin cheap pans vibrate more, because the layers move slightly against each other in the magnetic field. The fan running for a minute or two after you switch off is normal too. It's cooling the electronics. A slight crackle can also come from the pan. It usually shows up at high power with clad or thin bases, and sometimes as water starts to come to the boil. A quick way to check is to see whether it only happens with the noisy pans. If the cast iron pot never crackles, the crackle is probably from the pan as well. • Once the stockpot is cool, lay a straight edge across its base. If it rocks or there's a gap, a warped base will make it noisier.
• Use the zone that best matches the pot's size. • Cook at around 7 or 8 rather than full power or boost. You'll lose little speed and a lot of noise. The things that would change my view are the warning signs from before. Watch for loud sharp snapping rather than a faint crackle, a burning smell, sparks, the hob cutting out or showing a code, or noise from underneath with no pan on. If any of those appear, stop using it and switch it off at the isolator, then get an engineer in.

candidates: Normal induction noise from the pan at high power (vibration in multi-layer or heavy cookware) (high)
Cookware not ideal (warped, thin or loose-layered base, or not fully covering the zone) making the noise louder (medium)
Developing fault in the zone's induction coil/power module or the cooling fan (low)

Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Bosch; model PUE611BB1E.
The fault they reported is: "loud buzzing/humming noise on high". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
